title: The Garden Weasel

jokes.text: You folks see that flashing sign up there? Now, that sign says 'applesauce.' No, no, I'm kidding. It says 'applause.'
jokes.setup: Audience warm-up person points to the applause sign, claiming it says 'applesauce'
jokes.punchline: Immediately corrects himself — it says 'applause' — deflating the misdirection with total banality
jokes.explanation: A throwaway warm-up gag with minimal craft — the joke exists to establish the show-within-a-show framing rather than to be genuinely funny. The anti-joke structure (setting up something absurd and immediately deflating it) is mildly clever but lazy by design.

dialogue.speaker: Warm-up Host
dialogue.line: You folks see that flashing sign up there? Now, that sign says "applesauce." No, no, I'm kidding. It says "applause."

jokes.text: Thanks for coming to the show tonight. You are already so much better than last night's audience, who came in here and looted the place.
jokes.setup: Larry warmly thanks the audience for coming, complimenting them as 'so much better than last night's audience'
jokes.punchline: Last night's audience 'looted the place' — an absurd escalation from standard audience flattery
jokes.explanation: A solid monologue opening joke — the flattery-to-insult structure is well-worn but executed with good economy. The word 'looted' is the right choice; it's specific and absurd without trying too hard.

dialogue.line: And now, because only he brings out the natural luster of the wood... Larry Sanders!

jokes.text: I wanna thank them for returning the couch and Hank.
jokes.setup: Larry thanks last night's audience for looting the place
jokes.punchline: He thanks them for returning the couch and Hank — equating Hank with furniture as property that was stolen and returned
jokes.explanation: This is the better half of the two-part bit. Listing Hank alongside 'the couch' as stolen property is a sharp character-based joke that immediately establishes the Larry/Hank dynamic. The economy is excellent — it does double duty establishing Hank's low status with just one additional word.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You are already so much better than last night's audience... who came in here and looted the place. I wanna thank them for returning the couch and Hank.

jokes.text: How many of you saw Bill Clinton on Arsenio Hall when he played the sax? / Well, good to know you're watching my competition.
jokes.setup: Larry asks the audience if they saw Clinton on Arsenio Hall playing sax — the audience responds positively
jokes.punchline: Larry deadpans that it's 'good to know you're watching my competition' — self-deprecating acknowledgment that his audience is watching rivals
jokes.explanation: A timely, self-aware monologue joke grounded in the show's meta-context. Larry-as-late-night-host commenting on his competition feeds the show's satirical premise. The self-deprecation is slightly more interesting than the typical celebrity ribbing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, good to know you're watching my competition.

jokes.text: We had Jerry Brown on this show. He didn't actually play a number with the band, but he did score them some great coke.
jokes.setup: Clinton played sax on Arsenio; Larry pivots to his own guest Jerry Brown as a comparison
jokes.punchline: Brown didn't play with the band — he scored them coke instead, flipping the expected music punchline into a drug dealer twist
jokes.explanation: Strong misdirection — the setup primes the audience for a music-related punchline parallel to the Clinton sax joke, but lands on drug dealing. The subversive political humor is sharp for 1992. The structure is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm a little frustrated because we had Jerry Brown on this show. He didn't actually play a number with the band... but he did score them some great coke.

jokes.text: I was really leaning towards voting for the Captain of Captain and Tennille, because evidently, he at least has some military experience.
jokes.setup: Sonny Bono ran for Senate; Larry mocks California's celebrity political culture
jokes.punchline: He almost voted for the Captain from Captain and Tennille because of his 'military experience' — conflating a nautical stage persona with actual military credentials
jokes.explanation: A genuinely funny bit — the logic is absurdist but internally consistent. The joke rewards listeners who catch the double layer: 'The Captain' is a stage name, so treating it as military rank is delightfully stupid-smart. Elevated by the word 'evidently,' which nails the deadpan delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I was really leaning towards voting... for the Captain of Captain and Tennille... because evidently, he at least has some military experience.

jokes.text: Ted Kennedy got married this last weekend, and boy, he's gonna be in for a surprise when he sobers up, huh?
jokes.setup: Ted Kennedy's recent marriage announced as a news item
jokes.punchline: He'll be surprised when he sobers up — implying he was drunk when he agreed to marry
jokes.explanation: A fairly generic Kennedy-drinks joke. The formula is predictable — any comedian writing Kennedy material in 1992 would land in this neighborhood. It works in context but shows no distinctive craft.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Ted Kennedy got married this last weekend... and boy, he's gonna be in for a surprise when he sobers up, huh?

jokes.text: Did you like that joke, Hank? / I liked it very much. / Well, you're mistaken.
jokes.setup: Larry asks Hank on-air if he liked the Kennedy joke
jokes.punchline: Hank says he liked it very much; Larry immediately tells him 'Well, you're mistaken' — undermining Hank while simultaneously performing self-deprecation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. In three words ('Well, you're mistaken'), Larry performs self-aware self-deprecation, dismisses Hank's judgment as worthless, and establishes the asymmetric power dynamic between them — all simultaneously. The economy is exceptional. The character integration is nearly perfect: this is an exchange that could ONLY happen on a show where the host treats his sidekick as an unreliable subordinate. Comparable in compression to the 8.0 anchor example.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I liked it very much.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, you're mistaken.

jokes.text: The only reason I'm not running for president this year — I swear to God — is I am afraid no woman would come forward to say she had sex with me.
jokes.setup: In the context of the Clinton sex scandal era, Larry pivots to why he isn't running for president
jokes.punchline: He fears no woman would come forward to CLAIM they slept with him — inverting the political liability of sexual scandal into a pathetic admission of undesirability
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural inversion. The entire premise of 1992 political sex scandals is that women coming forward is damaging to politicians; Larry flips it to reveal the REAL indignity — nobody would bother. The joke is deeply character-specific to Larry's insecure, self-deprecating persona, making it feel authentic rather than a generic political bit. Strong originality for its era.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I swear, I feel I would be doing one of those CNN interviews... looking into the camera going, "Come on, Suzie. You know you did it with me. Say something."

jokes.text: I swear, I feel I would be doing one of those CNN interviews looking into the camera going, 'Come on, Suzie. You know you did it with me. Say something.'
jokes.setup: Larry extends the joke about no woman coming forward to claim sex with him
jokes.punchline: He imagines himself BEGGING a woman named 'Suzie' on CNN to validate their encounter — the pathetic specificity of 'Suzie' and the groveling desperation is the laugh
jokes.explanation: The escalation of joke #9 into a full dramatic scenario is well-executed. The name 'Suzie' (not 'Jennifer' or 'Susan' — 'Suzie') adds a specific pathetic intimacy. The image of a talk show host begging for sexual acknowledgment on CNN is richly absurd and character-specific. Slightly too wordy compared to #9 but the payoff earns the length.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: His Carol Channing was terrific.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It was.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You know, Patriot Games should have been a musical.

jokes.text: I didn't know Harrison Ford did impressions. His Carol Channing was terrific. / It was. You know, Patriot Games should have been a musical. He could have played all the parts.
jokes.setup: Post-show debrief; someone brings up Harrison Ford
jokes.punchline: Artie suggests Patriot Games should have been a musical and Ford could have played all the parts — an escalating absurdist flight that takes the Carol Channing impression joke to its logical extreme
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist riffing in the post-show debrief. The Carol Channing/Harrison Ford juxtaposition is inherently funny; Artie's escalation to 'he could have played all the parts' in a Patriot Games musical extends it nicely. The joke establishes the casual, insider comedy of the backstage world.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You could see her thigh between that short skirt and the boots?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I still see it.

jokes.text: Shirley Jones was gonna tell the story about Marty Ingels at K-Mart. / Perhaps she was nervous and forgot. / It doesn't matter. The woman's a babe.
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie discussing that Shirley Jones didn't get to tell her K-Mart story
jokes.punchline: Artie's polite 'Perhaps she was nervous and forgot' is immediately undercut by Larry's declaration that 'The woman's a babe' — dismissing the professional concern entirely for shallow appreciation
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Artie being diplomatic while Larry immediately pivots to ogling. The 'For God's sake' from someone (presumably Beverly or Artie) adds a well-timed straight-man beat. Character-specific and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: The monologue.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: There's a monologue in every show.

jokes.text: Remember in the Partridge Family? You could see her thigh between that short skirt and the boots? / I still see it.
jokes.setup: Larry is enthusing about Shirley Jones being a 'babe'; Hank recalls her Partridge Family look
jokes.punchline: 'I still see it' — Hank reveals he regularly conjures this mental image, which is simultaneously pathetic, funny, and perfectly Hank
jokes.explanation: 'I still see it' is a beautiful three-word character joke. The present tense implies ongoing fantasy recall, making it funnier and sadder than 'I remember it.' Perfectly Hank — shameless, oblivious, enthusiastic. High character integration score because this could ONLY be Hank Kingsley.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'll come over later and stick a red hot poker up your ass. We'll call it even.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Okay. You have my address, right?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And your poker size.

jokes.text: I hope no one heard that. / Good show tonight. / Like you saw it. / I watched it in your office. / Really? What was your favorite part? / The monologue. / There's a monologue in every show. / I really watched it tonight.
jokes.setup: Hank claims he watched the show; Larry calls him out
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'favorite part' was 'the monologue' — Larry's pointed 'There's a monologue in every show' exposes Hank as having watched nothing specific, then Hank's weak 'I really watched it tonight' makes it worse
jokes.explanation: A sharp escalating cringe sequence. 'There's a monologue in every show' is a devastating line — quietly the episode's best Larry-catches-Hank-lying moment. The structure is excellent: Hank digs himself in with each answer. Strong character integration because Hank's toadying obliviousness and Larry's cold precision are both perfectly deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A network president shouldn't be allowed to say Hello, Larry.

jokes.text: Network meeting. Come on. / No. No! / Come on. Come on. It's the network!
jokes.setup: Artie announces a network meeting
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate, childlike 'No. No!' followed by Artie's escalating 'It's the NETWORK!' as if volume will change the answer
jokes.explanation: Good functional character comedy establishing Larry's avoidance behavior and Artie's role as his wrangler. Not a laugh-out-loud moment but a solid character beat that seeds the episode's conflict.

dialogue.speaker: Sheldon
dialogue.line: What do we do to keep our advertisers happy... other than giving them free hand jobs?

jokes.text: Fuck me. I can't go. I'm not just saying this, Artie. I got a pain.
jokes.setup: Artie lists the network attendees, including the new VP Melanie Parish
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate hypochondriac escape attempt — 'I got a pain' — delivered with complete sincerity as a legitimate excuse to skip the network
jokes.explanation: Establishes Larry's cowardly hypochondria as a character trait. The 'I'm not just saying this' qualifier — which he absolutely IS just saying — is the funniest element. Functional character-building comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, you know, knowing the sponsors the way I do... I just think they would respond more to the hand jobs.

jokes.text: Fine. You just go home. I'll come over later and stick a red hot poker up your ass. We'll call it even. / Okay. You have my address, right? / And your poker size.
jokes.setup: Larry refuses to go to the network meeting; Artie threatens him with a red-hot poker
jokes.punchline: Larry responds 'Okay. You have my address, right?' — taking the threat completely straight — and Artie's 'And your poker size' is a perfectly absurd escalation implying he knows Larry's dimensions
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed exchange. Artie's threat is absurdly specific ('red hot poker'); Larry's acceptance of it as a reasonable arrangement is funnier than any protest would be; and 'Your poker size' from Artie implies a history of intimate knowledge that's simultaneously disturbing and hilarious. Strong Rip Torn energy — this is Artie's voice distinctly.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I didn't know that. Hank's the fucking Green Giant?

jokes.text: Hi, Shel. A network president shouldn't be allowed to say 'Hello, Larry.'
jokes.setup: Sheldon greets Larry with a casual 'Hello, Larry'
jokes.punchline: Larry points out the eerie coincidence that the network president's greeting is also the title of a specific (bad) TV show — implying it undermines his authority
jokes.explanation: A clever inside joke — 'Hello, Larry' was a spinoff of Diff'rent Strokes that was a notable failure. Larry pointing it out is both TV-insider comedy and a subtle power play. The meta layer (a talk show host referencing a bad TV show with his name) enriches it slightly.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Gee, I didn't know we were still owned by the garage-door opener people.

jokes.text: We're getting kicked in the balls. There's video markets. There's cable. It's trench warfare.
jokes.setup: Melanie delivers a corporate speech about the difficult economic climate of network television
jokes.punchline: The speech escalates from businesslike to military metaphor to 'kicked in the balls' — corporate jargon colliding with visceral vulgarity
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is situational — this is HBO in 1992, and a female VP saying 'kicked in the balls' in a corporate meeting is mildly transgressive. The trench warfare metaphor adds an appropriately absurd escalation. Functional scene-comedy, not a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That is no way to talk about Miss Parish.

jokes.text: What do we do to keep our advertisers happy, other than giving them free hand jobs?
jokes.setup: Melanie is running through strategies to retain advertiser relationships
jokes.punchline: She inserts 'other than giving them free hand jobs' as a rhetorical aside — treating sexual favors to sponsors as a baseline already-established strategy
jokes.explanation: The casual insertion of 'hand jobs' into corporate-speak is the joke — the implication that this is an accepted and ongoing practice that doesn't even merit comment. Economical and darkly funny. Establishes the show's willingness to go transgressive in a matter-of-fact way.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Garden Weasel, honey. It's the Garden Weasel.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The Garden Weasel.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Weasel's funnier.

jokes.text: Well, you know, knowing the sponsors the way I do, I just think they would respond more to the hand jobs.
jokes.setup: Melanie's pitch about live commercials lands; Larry needs to respond
jokes.punchline: Larry calls back Melanie's 'hand jobs' line by endorsing hand jobs as the superior sponsor-retention strategy — with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A well-timed callback that simultaneously shows Larry's avoidance mechanism (deflecting via joke rather than engaging with the problem), his relationship with Melanie (testing her), and his general tendency to treat his own wisecracks as superior strategies. The deadpan delivery implied by Garry Shandling's persona elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm sure that bitch Melanie's laughing her ass off.

jokes.text: I don't know if you know, but Hank Kingsley does a hell of a lot of fine commercial work. He does the adjustable bed. He does the medical alert necklace.
jokes.setup: The network wants Larry to do live commercials; Artie pivots to volunteering Hank
jokes.punchline: Artie's enthusiastic list of Hank's commercial credits — adjustable bed, medical alert necklace — are products associated with elderly, infirm or desperate people, painting Hank as a bottom-tier pitchman
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the specificity of the products — these are ads that run at 3 a.m., pitched by has-beens. Artie delivering this as a 'hell of a lot of fine commercial work' with genuine pride is perfectly sardonic. Character-specific to Artie's strategic maneuvering.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Artie said when we got out of the meeting... 'I swear I killed that woman in Korea.'

jokes.text: The thing is, Hank does too much commercial work. He's way overexposed. His saturation level is very high. / He's doing the Green Giant spots. / Is that Hank? / You can't really tell because you only see him from the knees down. / I didn't know that. Hank's the fucking Green Giant?
jokes.setup: Larry counterpitches to prevent Hank from doing the commercial; mentions the Green Giant ads as evidence of overexposure
jokes.punchline: Melanie's genuine surprise — 'Is that Hank?' — followed by 'You can't really tell because you only see him from the knees down' reveals the absurdly anonymous nature of the role, then 'Hank's the FUCKING Green Giant?' as the capper
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's highlights. The reveal that Hank is the Green Giant but 'you can only see him from the knees down' is a brilliantly specific humiliation — he's unrecognizable even in his own ad. Melanie's baffled 'Is that Hank?' and subsequent 'Hank's the FUCKING Green Giant?' are perfectly calibrated. The joke works on multiple levels: Hank's degraded celebrity status, the absurdity of the visual, and the corporate cluelessness of Melanie not knowing her own network's talent. Strong originality.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Honey, it's not your Make Me Laugh audition tape, is it?

jokes.text: And that comes directly from Unidac Electronics. / Gee, I didn't know we were still owned by the garage-door opener people.
jokes.setup: Melanie invokes the parent company Unidac Electronics as the ultimate authority demanding commercial compliance
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'garage-door opener people' — reducing the corporate overlord to a mundane product category with gentle contempt
jokes.explanation: A solid satirical jab at corporate media consolidation — the idea that a beloved TV show is ultimately controlled by garage-door opener manufacturers is funny because it was/is true. Larry's casual dismissiveness is well-pitched. Slightly weakened by Melanie's follow-up explanation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: From the Pan Am files. I was halfway to Fort Worth, when all of a sudden it hit me... I'd left my briefcase back at the terminal at JFK.

jokes.text: Yes, Mr. Sanders, they do still own you. They're a couple payments short, but that's another discussion.
jokes.setup: Larry dismisses Unidac; Melanie confirms they own him
jokes.punchline: 'They're a couple payments short, but that's another discussion' — the throwaway revelation that Larry hasn't been fully paid for is delivered as a minor bookkeeping note
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the casualness — Melanie mentions unpaid talent fees as a sidebar to the main discussion. The 'but that's another discussion' brush-off is perfectly in character for a network executive. A dark little industry joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm not in a position to say no. They'll think I'm an asshole. They'll think I'm not a team player.

jokes.text: What would the commercial be for? / The Garden Weasel. / That is no way to talk about Miss Parish.
jokes.setup: Larry asks what the commercial product is; the answer is 'The Garden Weasel'
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately interprets 'Garden Weasel' as an insult directed at Melanie — 'That is no way to talk about Miss Parish'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and arguably the best single line. The timing is perfect — the product name is announced, and before anyone can process it, Artie fires back with a protective gallantry that reads 'Garden Weasel' as a personal slur. The joke works because 'weasel' IS an insult, and because Artie's loyalty is expressed through this perfectly timed misdirection. Maximum economy — six words deliver the punchline. High quotability. This is a joke that would live in a highlight reel.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm a day away from just being the funny weather man in Tuscon. 'Oh, but on this good side, it's dry heat.'

jokes.text: The name alone is funny. / Garden Weasel, honey. It's the Garden Weasel. / Even funnier. / The Garden Weasel. / Weasel's funnier.
jokes.setup: At home, Jeannie tries to convince Larry the commercial is no big deal; she keeps saying the product name
jokes.punchline: Larry analyzes the comedic potential of 'Garden Weasel' with increasing precision — 'Weasel's funnier' — turning the word itself into a comedy exercise
jokes.explanation: A fun scene that does double duty — it's funny in itself (Larry as comedy critic breaking down why 'weasel' is funnier than 'garden') while establishing his relationship with Jeannie as warm and his professional anxiety as pervasive. The repetition of 'Garden Weasel' escalating to 'Weasel's funnier' is observationally correct and self-aware.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Paula says Robert Hays is booked on the show tonight... but he fell in the shower and he's seeing shapes and colors and stuff.

jokes.text: I'm sure that bitch Melanie's laughing her ass off.
jokes.setup: Larry is stewing about the Garden Weasel commercial assignment
jokes.punchline: The sudden venom — 'that bitch Melanie' — after a moment of seemingly processing the commercial like an adult is a character reveal disguised as an outburst
jokes.explanation: The sudden shift to paranoid hostility is funny and character-specific, but the line itself isn't particularly sharp. It works as a reveal of Larry's internal world but doesn't have memorable craft on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Perfect. I won't ask him anything tough.

jokes.text: She's not that bad. / She isn't that bad? / Artie said when we got out of the meeting, 'I swear I killed that woman in Korea.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie defends Melanie; Larry contests it by reporting Artie's line
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'I swear I killed that woman in Korea' — delivered as serious evidence that someone is not 'that bad' — is a perfectly absurd character reference
jokes.explanation: The first deployment of what becomes Artie's signature Korea line. Rip Torn's character being a Korean War veteran who literally believes he killed people he later encounters is one of the show's great running gags. This introductory instance is perfectly pitched — Larry uses it as evidence of Melanie's decency (or the opposite), which twists the logic beautifully. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Permission to speak freely?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Permission granted.

jokes.text: The fucking dog's at it again. / Would you act like a dog, for God's sakes? / Oh, honey. / He thinks he's doing good.
jokes.setup: The domestic scene is interrupted by the sound of the dog doing something
jokes.punchline: Larry's exasperation ('Would you act like a dog, for God's sakes?') followed by Jeannie's gentle defense ('He thinks he's doing good') implies the dog is engaged in some embarrassing sexual or destructive behavior
jokes.explanation: A light domestic beat. 'He thinks he's doing good' is mildly funny as a defense of presumably embarrassing dog behavior. Establishes the home environment but not a standout comedic moment.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That one Green Giant spot has really been a monkey on my back.

jokes.text: It's not your Make Me Laugh audition tape, is it? / No, but if you want to see that again, just... / You sure? Okay.
jokes.setup: Larry is about to show Jeannie an old commercial tape; she guesses what it might be
jokes.punchline: She guesses the Make Me Laugh audition tape — implying Larry has made her watch this humiliating artifact before — and Larry's 'if you want to see it again...' suggests he'd be delighted to
jokes.explanation: Make Me Laugh was a real game show — the reference lands because it's a slightly embarrassing credit in showbiz. Larry's eagerness to show it again is a nice character touch (he wants her validation even for embarrassing material). Functional cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Robert Hays
dialogue.line: Mommy? Mommy, why can't I ride the dog?

jokes.text: Don't look directly at the set, honey. This is a commercial I did in 1979.
jokes.setup: Larry is about to play his old Pan Am commercial
jokes.punchline: 'Don't look directly at the set' — treating his own old commercial like a solar eclipse or a weapon that requires protective measures
jokes.explanation: A lovely little character moment. 'Don't look directly at the set' implies the old commercial is so cringe-inducing that direct viewing is hazardous — like a shame bomb. Larry's self-awareness about his past work is funnier than simple embarrassment.

dialogue.speaker: Robert Hays
dialogue.line: Mommy? Mommy, why can't I ride the dog? I had you going, didn't I? I had you going.

jokes.text: The 1979 Pan Am commercial itself — Larry earnestly pitching Pan Am customer service using a lost-briefcase anecdote, ending with 'Can I get you anything else? / No thanks. You've already done more than enough.' / 'The art of flying.'
jokes.setup: Larry's '1979 vintage' commercial is played; we watch a young, sincere Larry pitch Pan Am
jokes.punchline: The commercial is essentially earnest corporate boosterism — 'The art of flying' tagline lands as pretentious and hollow after the mundane briefcase anecdote. The cringe is the gap between the self-important production and the trivial story.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is meta — we're watching a fake old commercial within a fake TV show, and the 'art of flying' tagline is funnier for being historically real (Pan Am used similar pretentious slogans). The contrast between the earnest 1979 Larry and the 1992 Larry watching it self-consciously is the source of the humor. Rewatch bonus for the layered self-referential quality.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I swear I killed her in the war.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You used that line yesterday.

jokes.text: If you don't want to do the Weasel thing, just... / I'm not in the mood for sex talk, honey.
jokes.setup: Jeannie says 'If you don't want to do the Weasel thing' (referring to the Garden Weasel commercial)
jokes.punchline: Larry hears sexual innuendo in 'do the Weasel thing' and shuts it down with 'I'm not in the mood for sex talk, honey'
jokes.explanation: A serviceable double-entendre gag. The joke is predictable — 'weasel' as innuendo was already in the air — but executed with good timing. Larry's prim 'I'm not in the mood for sex talk, honey' as a deflection is the better element, inverting typical TV-couple dynamics.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It's just that I don't even own a Garden Weasel. Never used one. It's a little unethical, don't you think?

jokes.text: They'll think I'm an asshole. They'll think I'm not a team player. Before you know it, I won't be able to get repairs made in the studio. I won't be able to get guests I want. Hank and I will be sharing an office. I'm a day away from just being the funny weather man in Tucson.
jokes.setup: Jeannie suggests Larry just tell the network he won't do the commercial
jokes.punchline: Larry's catastrophizing spirals from 'asshole' to 'sharing an office with Hank' to 'funny weather man in Tucson' — each step perfectly plausible in Larry's paranoid logic
jokes.explanation: Larry's anxiety spiral is excellent character comedy. The escalation is perfectly structured: each step is one degree more humiliating than the last, but 'sharing an office with Hank' is a sharper indignity than 'funny weather man in Tucson' in Larry's mind. 'Funny weather man in Tucson' has become a kind of show-business idiom for career death. 'Oh, but on this good side, it's dry heat' as the punchline extension is perfectly Larry — he can't help performing even in his own despair. High character integration: this spiral is the distilled essence of the character.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Unethical? Geez, Larry, don't start pulling at that thread. Our whole world will unravel.

jokes.text: 'Oh, but on the good side, it's dry heat.'
jokes.setup: Larry imagines himself as the 'funny weather man in Tucson' as the endpoint of career collapse
jokes.punchline: He immediately performs what that weather report would sound like — 'Oh, but on the good side, it's dry heat' — as a tiny, pathetic joke, which IS the joke
jokes.explanation: A masterful self-contained moment. Larry performs the worst version of his future self — a bad weather joke about dry heat — and in doing so both lampoons terrible TV humor AND reveals his deepest fear: becoming mediocre. The 'dry heat' gag is objectively bad, which makes it the point. The self-awareness of a comedian performing bad comedy to illustrate his fear of bad comedy is layered and character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, you know not what you applaud for.

jokes.text: Paula says Robert Hays is booked on the show tonight, but he fell in the shower and he's seeing shapes and colors and stuff. / Perfect. I won't ask him anything tough.
jokes.setup: Beverly delivers news that the guest Robert Hays (of Airplane! fame) is injured and hallucinating
jokes.punchline: Larry's response 'Perfect. I won't ask him anything tough' — treating a concussed, hallucinating guest as a gift rather than a problem
jokes.explanation: Sharp and cynical — perfectly captures the talk show host's relationship to guests: they're content delivery systems, not people. Larry's immediate pivot to 'how can I use this' is dark and funny. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, maybe you caught the reflection in that magnifying makeup mirror.

jokes.text: Excuse me, Larry. Hank would like to speak with you. / And you're clearing the way because Hank won't come in here on his own?
jokes.setup: An assistant announces Hank wants to speak with Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately deduces (correctly) that Hank needs to be escorted in — unable to simply walk through a door uninvited — and calls it out instantly
jokes.explanation: An excellent small character joke that establishes the Larry/Hank dynamic precisely. The implication is that Hank is so subordinate and intimidated that he can't enter his boss's office without permission — and Larry knows this about him so well he says it reflexively. This is the kind of show-don't-tell character work that elevates good writing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm about 100 yards off the green here. I'll try a five Weasel.

jokes.text: Did you, by any chance, feel an earthquake about 20 minutes ago? / I did not feel an earthquake. / Okay, but I think today is the day.
jokes.setup: Beverly asks about an earthquake; Larry flatly denies it
jokes.punchline: 'Okay, but I think today is the day' — Beverly's calm insistence that the Big One is coming today, delivered without alarm as a simple scheduling note
jokes.explanation: A dry background joke about LA earthquake anxiety. 'I think today is the day' as an end-of-civilization prediction delivered with clerical calm is a good deadpan moment. Slightly underwritten but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And by the way, it's been years since I've said that.

jokes.text: Larry, Darlene said you wanted to see me. / [Beat] What's on your mind, for God's sakes?
jokes.setup: Hank enters saying Darlene told him Larry wanted to see him — but Larry specifically said he DIDN'T want to see Hank, then said 'Tell Hank to come in'
jokes.punchline: The awkward beat as Larry processes that Hank has been told Larry summoned him (Larry didn't) and then Hank's nervous entrance — the comedy is in Hank's vulnerability and Larry's withering 'What's on your mind, for God's sakes'
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Hank being summoned to a meeting on false pretenses — having to come hat in hand when he thought he was invited — is a small bureaucratic humiliation. 'For God's sakes' as Larry's greeting telegraphs his contempt perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And by the way, it's been years since I've said that.

jokes.text: Permission to speak freely? / Permission granted.
jokes.setup: Hank wants to raise a sensitive topic with Larry
jokes.punchline: Hank uses military/institutional language ('Permission to speak freely') with Larry, who plays along by granting permission — the absurdity is that a TV sidekick needs to formally request permission to speak to his boss
jokes.explanation: Four words reveal the entire Larry/Hank power dynamic. Hank's use of military rank protocol with his TV boss — and Larry's complete comfort playing commanding officer — is both funny and a little sad. The economy is perfect. This exchange could only exist between these two characters.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I hit Jimmy Hoffa.

jokes.text: The thing is, it's a commercial for the Garden Weasel. / That's right. / I know the Garden Weasel. I use the Garden Weasel. / [pause] / And I have a good relationship with the Garden Weasel people. They're good people.
jokes.setup: Larry tells Hank the commercial is for the Garden Weasel; Hank processes this
jokes.punchline: Hank's escalating personal endorsements — 'I know the Garden Weasel. I use the Garden Weasel' — followed by the beat, then 'I have a good relationship with the Garden Weasel people. They're good people.' — Hank treating his customer relationship with a garden tool brand as a social reference
jokes.explanation: Jeffrey Tambor's Hank at his best. The three escalating Garden Weasel statements — I know it, I use it, they're good people — reveal a man who has cultivated professional relationships with bargain garden tools as social capital. The pause before 'good relationship with the Garden Weasel people' implies Hank is selecting his strongest qualification. Deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Melanie
dialogue.line: I feel quite certain our client didn't expect to hear... the name of a dead Teamster used as a selling point.

jokes.text: Well, Hank, I want you to know I told them I wanted you to do the spots. / And they said? / I don't remember what they said.
jokes.setup: Larry claims he recommended Hank for the commercial; Hank asks what the Garden Weasel people said in response
jokes.punchline: 'I don't remember what they said' — Larry's cover-up is so bad that he can't even invent a positive response; the implication is they said something deeply unflattering about Hank
jokes.explanation: One of the best exchanges in the episode. Larry's brutal honesty disguised as forgetfulness — 'I don't remember what they said' — is a perfect lie because it tells the whole truth. Of course he remembers. They said something terrible about Hank, and Larry would rather pretend amnesia than deliver the verdict. Hank's subsequent beat as he processes this is where the cringe comedy lives. The economy is exceptional: five words do the work of a monologue about how unwanted Hank is.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You know the truly frightening thing?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm really turned on right now.

jokes.text: That one Green Giant spot has really been a monkey on my back. / I'll tell you one thing: If they ever ask you to put on a pair of green tights, no matter how much they offer you, you just walk away. / Walk away.
jokes.setup: Hank laments that the Green Giant spot has hurt his career; Larry offers advice
jokes.punchline: Larry's sage counsel about not wearing green tights — treating it as hard-won wisdom like 'never go with a stranger to a second location' — and the solemn repetition 'Walk away' treats the green tights as a career-destroying moral hazard
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Green Giant revelation works beautifully — now we're in Hank's perspective on it. Larry delivering 'walk away' as ancient Hollywood wisdom (with the implicit repetition emphasizing gravity) is both character-perfect and funny. The advice is so specific as to be absurd but also genuinely applicable only to someone like Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I understand that. I used to be single.

jokes.text: Are you sure you're feeling up to this, Mr. Hays? / I'm fine. / We can always reschedule you. / I'm fine. / Oh, my God! Are you okay? Do you want me to call a doctor? / Mommy? Mommy, why can't I ride the dog?
jokes.setup: Staff members are concerned about the injured Robert Hays; Hays insists he's fine
jokes.punchline: The staff member screams in alarm — and Hays immediately drops the hallucination to deliver 'Mommy? Mommy, why can't I ride the dog?' — a perfect non-sequitur that both confirms the injury AND turns out to be a setup for his next revelation that it was a joke
jokes.explanation: 'Why can't I ride the dog?' is a brilliant non-sequitur — specific enough to be funny (why a DOG? why RIDING?) while perfectly evoking the randomness of a concussed mind. The double reveal (is he really injured? no, he's joking) adds structural complexity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I understand that. I used to be single.

jokes.text: I had you going, didn't I? I had you going. / That's really funny, Robert. / Well, I was in Airplane 2.
jokes.setup: Robert Hays reveals his hallucination was a joke and seeks validation
jokes.punchline: 'Well, I was in Airplane 2' — using his comedy film credit as qualification for pulling off a physical comedy bit, with the implicit acknowledgment that Airplane 2 (not Airplane!) is a slightly lesser credential
jokes.explanation: Excellent insider joke. 'I was in Airplane 2' as a comedy credential is funny because (a) it's the sequel, not the classic original, (b) it's used to justify a mediocre prank, and (c) Robert Hays actually WAS in Airplane! — so the show is gently roasting him by downgrading him to the sequel in his own self-citation. Sharp and specific.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You tell that Korean woman that she's wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: She is not Korean. Everybody thinks she's Korean.

jokes.text: Look who's here. Don't look. I think she saw you look.
jokes.setup: Artie spots Melanie Parish; tells Larry to be subtle
jokes.punchline: 'I think she saw you look' — the immediate defeat of the subtlety instruction, implying Larry immediately looked
jokes.explanation: A minor transitional beat. Functional but not distinctive — the 'don't look / she saw you look' structure is familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Why not just call it the Amazing Rat Stick?

jokes.text: I swear I killed her in the war. / You used that line yesterday. / It's not a line. It's a real concern.
jokes.setup: Artie repeats his Korea line about Melanie; Larry calls him on the repetition
jokes.punchline: 'It's not a line. It's a real concern.' — Artie's absolute insistence that his Korea assassination belief is not a rhetorical device but a genuine factual concern
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best running gag payoff. Larry calling it a 'line' and Artie's correction — 'It's not a line. It's a real concern.' — transforms a throwaway reference into a character philosophy. Artie genuinely believes this. The joke works because Rip Torn's Artie is exactly the kind of man who WOULD have made kills in Korea and WOULD track them into civilian life. The economy is exceptional: six words that define a character. High quotability — 'It's not a line. It's a real concern.' is the episode's most memorable exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Should I have said the Fabulous Vermin Instrument?

jokes.text: I don't feel right about doing this commercial. / You don't want to do it? Just say the word. I'll take care of it. / I'll take a shot at it. / It's just that I don't even own a Garden Weasel. Never used one. It's a little unethical, don't you think? / Unethical? Geez, Larry, don't start pulling at that thread. Our whole world will unravel.
jokes.setup: Larry raises an ethical concern about pitching a product he doesn't own or use
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'don't start pulling at that thread, our whole world will unravel' — treating advertising ethics as a dangerous Jenga piece that, if touched, will bring down the entire industry edifice
jokes.explanation: A sharp industry satire moment. 'Don't start pulling at that thread, our whole world will unravel' is a great line — it's Artie's world-weary acknowledgment that advertising/celebrity endorsement is fundamentally fraudulent AND his advice that this is a perfectly acceptable state of affairs to live with. The line is quotable, philosophically rich, and perfectly in Artie's voice.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If you were a guy, I'd take you outside right now.

dialogue.speaker: Melanie
dialogue.line: If you were a guy, I'd go.

jokes.text: Unethical? Geez, Larry, don't start pulling at that thread. Our whole world will unravel.
jokes.setup: Larry raises the ethical concern of endorsing a product he doesn't use
jokes.punchline: Artie warns that examining ethics in this industry is an existential threat — 'our whole world will unravel' — treating ethical inquiry as the genuine danger rather than unethical behavior
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best lines and a perfect encapsulation of what The Larry Sanders Show is about as a satire. 'Don't start pulling at that thread. Our whole world will unravel' is a pithy statement of Hollywood's entire ethical structure — built on convenient blindness, maintained by mutual agreement not to look too closely. The economy is exceptional, the character integration is perfect (only Artie would say this with this level of casual authority), and the line has genuine staying power as a quotable. This approaches the craft level of the 8.0 anchor and arguably exceeds it in concept.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I was tying my shoes this morning... I walked into the door, bumped my head.

dialogue.speaker: Melanie
dialogue.line: Whatever.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, that's what really happened.

dialogue.speaker: Melanie
dialogue.line: All right, a woman hit me.

jokes.text: How are you feeling? Didn't you, by the way, fall? I know you were almost gonna cancel tonight. You fell in the shower? Is that it?
jokes.setup: Larry interviews Robert Hays on-air about the shower incident
jokes.punchline: Larry's rapid-fire, slightly invasive interrogation ('Didn't you, by the way, fall?') combines faux-concern with avid prying — the talk show host mining a guest's embarrassment for content with only the thinnest veneer of sympathy
jokes.explanation: Functional on-air cringe — the mock-interview lets us see Larry as a predatory talk show host. Not a standout moment but establishes the show-within-the-show's satirical texture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I was tying my shoes this morning... I walked into the door, bumped my head.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Whatever.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, that's what really happened.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: All right, a woman hit me.

jokes.text: I was standing there, dripping wet, stark naked. / [audience laughs] / If you men could please just settle down.
jokes.setup: Robert Hays describes standing naked in the bathroom
jokes.punchline: The audience responds to 'stark naked' and Larry's dry 'If you men could please just settle down' — treating the male audience members' excitement about male nudity as an audience management problem
jokes.explanation: Larry's aside to the (all-male, apparently) crowd getting excited about male nudity is a quick, dry inversion gag. Works in the mock-talk-show context as an unexpected host-management moment.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: America. Everything she stands for.

jokes.text: Geez! Well, I'll end up... I'll send Hank out there dripping wet. / Yeah, you know not what you applaud for.
jokes.setup: Audience continues applauding the naked imagery; Larry threatens to send Hank out dripping wet
jokes.punchline: 'You know not what you applaud for' — Larry's philosophical audience warning that if they want nudity, they'll get Hank's nudity, which is presumably much worse
jokes.explanation: 'You know not what you applaud for' is a nicely formal phrasing for what is essentially a crude threat about Hank's naked body. The implied horror of Hank in the nude is funnier for being unspoken.

dialogue.speaker: Audience
dialogue.line: Hello, Garden Weasel!

jokes.text: I dropped the towel. I bent over to pick it up, and I saw the reflection in the mirror. It kind of shocked me. I stood up, slipped, and... / Well, maybe you caught the reflection in that magnifying makeup mirror.
jokes.setup: Hays explains he was shocked by his own reflection in the bathroom, which caused the fall
jokes.punchline: Larry offers 'maybe you caught the reflection in that magnifying makeup mirror' — suggesting Hays's horror was caused by a magnified view of his own anatomy
jokes.explanation: A good subversive joke — the magnifying makeup mirror implication (seeing his genitalia enlarged and being horrified by it) is left tastefully implicit while being perfectly clear. The suggestion is both darkly funny and appropriately transgressive for HBO.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: This Garden Weasel does the work of ten men and a boy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: How many boys, Hank?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: One small boy.

jokes.text: Didn't you get those little flower applique things I sent you? I sent you a whole pack that you're supposed to stick on. I stick them to the bottom of my feet so you don't slide anywhere.
jokes.setup: Larry is discussing bathroom safety following the shower accident narrative
jokes.punchline: Larry's confession that he puts shower-safety flower appliques on the BOTTOMS OF HIS FEET rather than the shower floor — a completely wrong but earnestly held safety solution
jokes.explanation: Delightfully absurd. The image of Larry Sanders padding around with flower stickers on the soles of his feet — having fundamentally misunderstood how shower appliques work — is both funny and character-revealing (he's safety-anxious and slightly neurotic). The 'I sent you a whole pack' implies he evangelizes this wrong solution to friends, which deepens the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And if Unidac Electronics has a little problem with this... they can screw a lightbulb up my ass and use me as a desk lamp.

jokes.text: You go into a public shower... What? Commercial? — We have to take a commercial. — Do we? So what else? Anything else we need to know?
jokes.setup: Larry is mid-anecdote about public showers; the segment producer signals commercial break
jokes.punchline: Larry's reaction — 'Do we? So what else? Anything else we need to know?' — as if the commercial break is an arbitrary interruption of his important shower-safety speech
jokes.explanation: The meta-irony that the commercial break is interrupting a conversation about the very commercial Larry doesn't want to do — and his feigned surprise at having to take a break — is a nice structural touch. 'Anything else we need to know?' is a good line.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Don't take this as a threat, but I killed a man like you in Korea... hand to hand.

jokes.text: I want to welcome a new sponsor to The Larry Sanders Show... I'd like to... welcome you to the world of the Garden Weasel.
jokes.setup: Larry begins the live Garden Weasel commercial, clearly deeply uncomfortable
jokes.punchline: The extended pause and awkward restart ('I'd like to...') before 'welcome you to the world of the Garden Weasel' — the comedy of a talk show host visibly struggling to pretend he inhabits the world of a garden tool
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely situational — we know Larry hates this, we see him failing to commit. The cringe value is high but the craft is in the performance rather than the writing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Don't take this as a threat, but I killed a man like you in Korea... hand to hand.

jokes.text: You know, if you've got a green thumb — and by the way, if you do, I know a specialist...
jokes.setup: Larry tries to deliver the Garden Weasel copy: 'if you've got a green thumb...'
jokes.punchline: He can't help editorializing — 'if you do, I know a specialist' — treating the gardening metaphor 'green thumb' literally as a medical condition requiring referral
jokes.explanation: A nice bit of Larry subverting the commercial copy by taking the idiom literally. The aside is quick and well-timed — he treats 'green thumb' as a medical condition requiring specialist referral, which is both absurd and character-perfect (Larry riffing rather than reading straight copy).

jokes.text: Let's see. I'm about 100 yards off the green here. / I'll try a five Weasel.
jokes.setup: Larry is supposed to demonstrate the Garden Weasel's gardening utility
jokes.punchline: He shifts to a golf metaphor — 'I'm about 100 yards off the green' and 'I'll try a five Weasel' — treating the Garden Weasel as a golf club and the garden as a golf course
jokes.explanation: A strong absurdist bit — Larry's total inability to stay in the gardening frame leads him to golf, which feels true to his character (a Hollywood guy who golfs more than he gardens). 'A five Weasel' as a club selection has a very specific absurdist logic. The joke builds nicely.

jokes.text: No more weeding on your hands and knees. You just gently glide your Weasel. / And by the way, it's been years since I've said that.
jokes.setup: Larry reads copy about 'gently gliding your Weasel'
jokes.punchline: 'By the way, it's been years since I've said that' — Larry acknowledging the sexual innuendo in the product instructions as a personal confession
jokes.explanation: The Weasel-as-innuendo thread pays off nicely here. 'It's been years since I've said that' is both a good line and a character reveal about Larry's sex life (tying back to the 'no woman would claim to have slept with me' monologue jokes). The economy is good.

jokes.text: 'Look, Ma, I'm making valuable mulch.'
jokes.setup: Larry is demonstrating the Garden Weasel turning weeds into mulch
jokes.punchline: 'Look, Ma, I'm making valuable mulch' — a childlike cry of triumph delivered in an exaggeratedly excited voice, treating the mulch production as a childhood achievement
jokes.explanation: The 'Look, Ma!' structure applied to 'valuable mulch' is a good absurdist beat — the mock-childlike enthusiasm for dirt processing is inherently funny. Works in the commercial-destruction sequence.

jokes.text: Hello, Mr. Hoffa. / I hit Jimmy Hoffa.
jokes.setup: Larry is using the Garden Weasel in the garden soil; something hits with a clunk
jokes.punchline: He greets it as 'Mr. Hoffa' and then announces he hit Jimmy Hoffa — the punchline being that Jimmy Hoffa's body (famously rumored to be buried in a New Jersey meadow or similar) has been discovered in this garden
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup — Larry weaseling through dirt and striking something — is perfect for the Hoffa punchline. 'Hello, Mr. Hoffa' / 'I hit Jimmy Hoffa' is as economical as it gets. The Hoffa-buried-in-a-garden premise is original, dark, perfectly timed, and lands as a total surprise. The joke also works as a meta-commentary on the commercial's self-destruction — this is what happens when you let Larry Sanders freestyle. High quotability and originality.

jokes.text: A few glitches, but overall a terrific show. / Very funny. / Oh, Miss Parish. We need to talk. / Sure. I thought the commercial went great. I managed to say mulch and...
jokes.setup: Artie assesses the show after the Garden Weasel commercial disaster; Melanie arrives angry
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I thought the commercial went great. I managed to say mulch...' — citing 'managed to say mulch' as evidence of commercial success, the bar being set comically low
jokes.explanation: Larry's self-assessment criteria — 'I managed to say mulch' — is a perfectly calibrated lowering of expectations. After finding Jimmy Hoffa in the garden, successfully using the word 'mulch' IS an achievement. The gap between Larry's assessment and reality is the joke.

jokes.text: I managed to say mulch and... — What you did out there just now was in no way, shape or form remotely like an acceptable commercial spot.
jokes.setup: Larry tries to put a positive spin on the commercial disaster
jokes.punchline: Melanie's absolute brick-wall response — 'in no way, shape or form remotely like' — shuts down Larry's 'I said mulch' self-congratulation instantly
jokes.explanation: Larry's proud 'I managed to say mulch' is a beautiful piece of self-delusion; Melanie's comprehensive negation is well-timed. The comedy is in Larry's completely misaligned self-assessment.

jokes.text: I feel quite certain our client didn't expect to hear the name of a dead Teamster used as a selling point.
jokes.setup: Melanie is dressing Larry down for the disastrous commercial
jokes.punchline: 'The name of a dead Teamster used as a selling point' — framing the Hoffa gag as a marketing methodology concern, as if the problem is simply that Hoffa is dead (not that he was murdered by the mob)
jokes.explanation: 'Dead Teamster used as a selling point' is a good corporate-euphemism line. The official complaint focuses on Hoffa's role as a 'selling point' rather than the fact that he's a mob-connected crime figure whose probable murder is being mined for gardening humor. Nice understatement.

jokes.text: Rumor has it this is a very funny guy. When you ask Larry Sanders to do a commercial, you get Larry Sanders.
jokes.setup: Artie defends Larry against Melanie's criticism of the commercial
jokes.punchline: 'When you ask Larry Sanders to do a commercial, you get Larry Sanders' — framing Larry's inability to follow copy as a premium feature rather than a liability
jokes.explanation: Artie's spin is a good piece of showbiz logic — the defense that Larry's uncontrollability is his brand works as both satire of talent management and genuine character advocacy. The line is quotable and captures Artie's role perfectly.

jokes.text: You know the truly frightening thing? / What? / I'm really turned on right now.
jokes.setup: Melanie has just berated and left; Larry and Artie assess the encounter
jokes.punchline: Larry's confession that he's 'really turned on right now' — revealing that Melanie's aggression has sexually excited him
jokes.explanation: A sharp character moment. Larry's arousal by Melanie's dominance reveals his complicated psychology — the same insecurity that makes him fear powerful women also attracts him to them. 'The truly frightening thing' as a setup creates perfect expectation (we expect self-pity or industry analysis) and the subversion to sexual excitement is funny and character-rich.

jokes.text: Do you think you can deprogram him? / Well, it's not really deprogramming. It's behavior modification through positive reinforcement and treats. / I understand that. I used to be single.
jokes.setup: Someone asks if the dog trainer can 'deprogram' the dog; the trainer explains it's behavior modification through 'positive reinforcement and treats'
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'I understand that. I used to be single.' — applying dog-training methodology to his own past relationships with women, implying he managed women with the same techniques
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The misdirection is perfect — the question is about a dog, the answer is about the dog, and then Artie's aside connects dog training to dating with complete casual confidence. 'I used to be single' as the bridge makes the implication that single life required the same treat-based manipulation one uses with animals. The joke is offensive, absurdist, character-perfect for Artie, and delivered with ideal economy. Rip Torn could make this joke sing. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: What behavior do you want me to correct? / All of it.
jokes.setup: The dog trainer asks what specific behavior to correct
jokes.punchline: 'All of it.' — Artie's total, exhausted assessment that the dog needs complete behavioral overhaul
jokes.explanation: Economy is the entire joke. 'All of it' as the answer to what behavior to correct is perfectly bleak. Good laugh — simple and well-placed. Could apply to the dog, to Larry, to the show, to everything.

jokes.text: By the way, I bought a Garden Weasel this morning, and I love it. / Did you see the commercial? / It was very funny. / Wasn't that funny? You see, honey, that's two of us.
jokes.setup: Robert Hays casually mentions he bought a Garden Weasel that morning
jokes.punchline: The implication that the disastrous commercial actually SOLD a Garden Weasel — to a guest on the show, no less — is a perfect ironic validation of Larry's chaos
jokes.explanation: A nice structural callback — the commercial that Melanie called a disaster apparently worked, at least on Robert Hays. Larry's 'that's two of us' (implying he also bought one, or just celebrating any validation) is a small but warm ironic moment.

jokes.text: You tell that Korean woman that she's wrong. / She is not Korean. Everybody thinks she's Korean.
jokes.setup: Larry refers to Melanie as 'that Korean woman'; Jeannie corrects him
jokes.punchline: 'She is not Korean. Everybody thinks she's Korean.' — the reveal that this is a widespread misconception, implying a pattern of casual ethnic misidentification among the show's circle
jokes.explanation: Mildly dated in its comedy premise. The joke is essentially about casual racial misidentification as a running joke — works as a character beat showing Larry's casual prejudice and the social circle's shared blind spots, but not particularly sharp or original.

jokes.text: My God, a somersault! Where did you get this dog? / Well, we had a trainer on my show. He had a wonderful dog act, and then I fell in love with the dog. / Bill was getting ready to retire. / Bill Acres? / Yeah, I think that was it. Bill Acres, yeah. / I'm sorry, but no. This is a superbly trained animal. I can't touch him. That would be like painting over a Picasso. / I'm sorry. I have to leave.
jokes.setup: The dog does a somersault; this leads to a conversation about the dog's trainer and eventual ownership
jokes.punchline: Artie declaring the dog 'a Picasso' that cannot be altered, then immediately leaving — the comedy of an old Hollywood man treating a dog's training as sacred art and departing rather than argue the point
jokes.explanation: The dog-Picasso comparison is a funny piece of Artie logic — treating animal training as fine art. 'I'm sorry. I have to leave.' as an exit after failing to win the argument is good physical comedy. The scene is slightly loose but has good absurdist texture.

jokes.text: Chopper. / Door.
jokes.setup: The dog and Artie are presumably near a door; Artie commands the dog
jokes.punchline: The dog apparently opens the door on command — the comedy is in Artie's one-word commands and the dog's compliance, treated as completely ordinary
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — two words. Artie's terse 'Chopper. Door.' establishes that (1) the dog is named Chopper (perfect), (2) the dog opens doors, and (3) Artie communicates with animals in the same clipped manner he communicates with humans. A small but perfect visual beat that rewards rewatching.

jokes.text: And the patented tilling action digs deep into the soil and aerates all the way down to the roots. / You know, here's something I don't understand. Weasels. Aren't they rodents? Why would you name something after a rodent?
jokes.setup: Second Garden Weasel commercial; Larry is reading copy about the tilling action
jokes.punchline: Larry breaks character to question the fundamental naming logic of the Garden Weasel — 'Aren't they rodents? Why would you name something after a rodent?' — treating this as a genuine etymological problem mid-commercial
jokes.explanation: Larry's mid-commercial tangent into zoology is a good escalation of his inability to stay on-script. The observation is legitimately funny — weasels ARE somewhat unpleasant creatures to name a garden tool after. His earnestness about the branding concern is the comic core.

jokes.text: I mean, think about it. It's not a nice thing. Why not just call it the Amazing Rat Stick? / The Amazing Rat Stick? / Too far? / Should I have said the Fabulous Vermin Instrument?
jokes.setup: Larry proposes alternative rodent-based names for garden tools
jokes.punchline: 'The Fabulous Vermin Instrument' — a triumphantly absurd escalation that is both funnier and worse than 'Amazing Rat Stick', with the word 'Fabulous' doing impossible lifting
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'Amazing Rat Stick' to 'Fabulous Vermin Instrument' is well-structured — each alternative is worse than the last while being more elaborate. 'Fabulous Vermin Instrument' has excellent comedic rhythm and is genuinely quotable. Larry's self-questioning ('Too far?') adds a nice self-aware beat before he escalates further.

jokes.text: I'm doing the best I can. Other than that, I stuck to the copy. / Do you want me to fuck with your budget? Is that what you want me to do?
jokes.setup: Larry is being challenged on his commercial deviations
jokes.punchline: Larry defending himself — 'I stuck to the copy, other than [naming the Weasel after vermin]' — and then threatening to 'fuck with the budget' as a negotiating position, implying he has power he clearly doesn't have
jokes.explanation: Larry's bluster ('Do you want me to fuck with your budget?') as a defensive move is revealing — he has no actual leverage here, and the threat is empty. The comedy is in the gap between his tone and his position.

jokes.text: Boy, you know, don't ever come on to my set and talk to me like that in front of my people again. / I pay your people, my friend, and I pay you. I can talk to you any damn way I see fit! / What is your problem, exactly? I don't think this is about the commercial. I don't think you like me. I don't think you like my show. / It's not my favorite, but let's talk about problems.
jokes.setup: Larry confronts Melanie about her behavior; she escalates; he asks what her real problem is
jokes.punchline: 'It's not my favorite, but let's talk about problems' — Melanie's casual admission that she doesn't like Larry's show, delivered as a throwaway before moving to business
jokes.explanation: 'It's not my favorite, but let's talk about problems' is a perfect network-executive line. The admission is devastating and delivered without affect — she's not trying to hurt Larry, she just genuinely doesn't like the show and considers it a minor data point. The casualness of the delivery is what makes it cut.

jokes.text: What's your problem? I think it bugs you to take orders from a woman. / If you were a guy, I'd take you outside right now. / If you were a guy, I'd go. / As a rule, I don't hit women. / But this rule doesn't apply.
jokes.setup: Melanie accuses Larry of sexism; the confrontation escalates
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'But this rule doesn't apply' — after establishing he has a rule against hitting women, he exempts Melanie, suggesting he would in fact hit her
jokes.explanation: Artie's threat is funny because of its logical structure (I have a rule / the rule has exceptions / you're an exception) and because it's completely in character for the violent, Korea-traumatized Artie who believes he already killed Melanie once. The dark comedy of an old man threatening a network executive with physical violence is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: You don't have any problems with women. How many times have you been married? / How many times have you slept with Sheldon?
jokes.setup: Melanie tries to use Artie's marriage history as evidence against his sexism claims
jokes.punchline: Artie pivots immediately to 'How many times have you slept with Sheldon?' — transforming her rhetorical point into an accusation about her relationship with the network president
jokes.explanation: A sharp and vicious rhetorical move. Artie neutralizes Melanie's question (how many times married?) with a perfectly parallel counter-attack (how many times with Sheldon?) that implies her professional power is sexual. The question is deeply transgressive, perfectly timed, and completely in Artie's character as someone who operates without conventional workplace restraint. The parallel structure makes the exchange feel like a formal debate fought with knives.

jokes.text: That's a beauty. / I know. I was tying my shoes this morning, I walked into the door, bumped my head. / No, that's what really happened. / All right, a woman hit me.
jokes.setup: Larry compliments Artie's 'How many times with Sheldon' line; they separate and Larry ends up with a black eye
jokes.punchline: The fast-forward reveal that Melanie hit Artie — and his pathetic cover story ('I walked into a door') followed by the defeated 'All right, a woman hit me' — lands the escalation of the Artie/Melanie conflict
jokes.explanation: The reveal of the black eye and Artie's cover story is a solid payoff to the escalating confrontation. 'All right, a woman hit me' has good resigned energy. The structure is a bit predictable but the character-specific delivery (Artie refusing to admit it until cornered) elevates it.

jokes.text: How many times have you been married? / Well, everyone in the loop knows. / You're kidding? / Hey, guys. / Hey, Hank. / Whoa, what a shiner! What happened to you? / Melanie Parish hit me. / No, really. Softball? Doorknob?
jokes.setup: Word has gotten out about Artie's black eye; Hank arrives and asks innocently
jokes.punchline: Artie says 'Melanie Parish hit me' and Hank immediately defaults to 'Softball? Doorknob?' — refusing to believe a woman hit Artie and offering face-saving alternatives
jokes.explanation: Hank's 'Softball? Doorknob?' is a good character beat — he's offering Artie a polite fiction, which is also (accidentally) the kindest thing Hank does in the episode. The word pairing 'Softball? Doorknob?' is well-chosen for being the two most plausible/least shameful alternatives. Hank's oblivious gallantry works.

jokes.text: Can I ask you something about these commercials? I don't know what the heck I'm doing out there. I need a little advice. You've done, like, 20,000 of these things. Tell me something.
jokes.setup: Larry asks Hank for commercial advice — the host asking the sidekick for guidance
jokes.punchline: 'You've done, like, 20,000 of these things' — the figure 20,000 is an implied insult (how desperate for work do you have to be to do 20,000 commercials?) delivered as a compliment
jokes.explanation: The subtle double-edge of '20,000 commercials' as both a credential and an indictment of Hank's career choices is funny but understated. Primarily a scene-setter for the Hank commercial-wisdom sequence.

jokes.text: What happened to you? Melanie Parish hit me. No, really. Softball? Doorknob? Doorknob. Oh.
jokes.setup: Hank sees Artie's shiner and asks what happened, having been told 'Melanie hit me'
jokes.punchline: Hank reflexively disbelieves a woman hit Artie — offers 'Softball? Doorknob?' as alternatives — Artie caves to 'Doorknob' rather than maintain the truth, then Hank accepts it with a neutral 'Oh'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured small scene. Hank's instinctive 'No, really' at 'Melanie hit me' — followed by offering alternative explanations — and Artie choosing 'Doorknob' to avoid the humiliation of admitting a woman hit him, then Hank's flat 'Oh' as full acceptance — is a perfect three-beat cringe comedy sequence. Economy is excellent. The specificity of 'Softball? Doorknob?' as the two options offered is funny on its own. Hank's 'Oh' as a complete close is very Tambor.

jokes.text: Now, if you don't believe in your product, you gotta substitute something you do believe in. For instance, when I'm out there pitching the pearl cream that keeps you looking young... / Do you know what I'm thinking? / You're not thinking about the cream? / No, sir, I'm not. / What are you thinking about? / America. / Everything she stands for.
jokes.setup: Hank explains his commercial technique — substituting genuine belief for product belief
jokes.punchline: Hank reveals that when pitching wrinkle cream, he thinks about America — 'Everything she stands for.' — treating the republic as an emotional substitution for pearl cream
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes — possibly the best character joke for Hank. The technique of substituting genuine belief is a real acting/sales technique; Hank applies it magnificently by substituting AMERICA for wrinkle cream. The reveal — 'America. Everything she stands for.' — is delivered with complete sincerity and is hilarious precisely because it's not ironic for Hank. He genuinely loves America and uses that love to sell pearl cream. This is peak Hank Kingsley: simultaneously absurd, earnest, and revealing of a man who has found peace with his compromises by wrapping them in patriotism. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft.

jokes.text: Hank doing the Garden Weasel commercial — 'Friends, you say you love those fresh flowers and veggies, but you're tired of the aches and pains that come with weeding? Well, I'm here to tell you your weeding days are over. Can I hear you say, Hey now? / Hey now! / Pretty good. But can I hear you say, Hey now?'
jokes.setup: Hank takes over the commercial, deploying his full arsenal of crowd-work and evangelical salesmanship
jokes.punchline: Hank gets the audience to say 'Hey now' as part of a Garden Weasel commercial — his signature catchphrase repurposed as commercial call-and-response, revealing the catchphrase has always been about controlling audiences rather than genuine warmth
jokes.explanation: Hank in his natural habitat — leading a crowd in call-and-response, feeling the love, his catchphrase doing double duty as gardening enthusiasm. The comedy is in the incongruity of evangelical preacher energy applied to a garden tool, and in how GOOD Hank is at it compared to how bad Larry was. The character contrast is the joke.

jokes.text: I have here in my hands... well, it's a miracle of gardening engineering. Ladies and gentlemen, say hello to the Garden Weasel. / Hello, Garden Weasel!
jokes.setup: Hank presents the Garden Weasel to the audience as if introducing a celebrity
jokes.punchline: The audience responds 'Hello, Garden Weasel!' — treating a garden tool as a personage worthy of a crowd greeting
jokes.explanation: The audience being led to formally greet a garden implement is a good absurdist beat. Hank's framing of the Weasel as a celebrity arrival ('say hello to...') and the audience compliance is funny, and it shows how the audience responds to Hank's performative mastery.

jokes.text: This Garden Weasel does the work of ten men and a boy. How many boys, Hank? One small boy.
jokes.setup: Hank's enthusiastic commercial claim: 'the work of ten men and a boy'
jokes.punchline: Larry's interrogation of the 'boy' specification, answered with precise specificity: 'One small boy' — the absurdist exactness of the measurement unit
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's great jokes. 'Ten men and a boy' is already an archaic, funny unit of measurement. Larry's probe ('How many boys?') opens an absurd taxonomic door, and Hank's instant, specific 'One small boy' — as if this is established agricultural data — is perfect. The comedy lives in the deadpan precision: not 'a boy,' not 'one boy,' but 'one SMALL boy.' The size specification implies there are labor tables for boy sizes somewhere. Maximum economy: three words for an enormous laugh. This belongs in any highlight reel of the series.

jokes.text: This Garden Weasel does the work of ten men and a boy. / How many boys, Hank? / One small boy.
jokes.setup: Hank claims the Garden Weasel does 'the work of ten men and a boy'
jokes.punchline: Larry interrupts to ask 'How many boys, Hank?' — treating it as an ambiguous specification — and Hank's precise 'One small boy' is the perfect answer
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. Larry's question ('How many boys, Hank?') is absurdist and perfectly timed — treating 'a boy' in the idiom as a specific quantity requiring clarification. Hank's answer 'One small boy' completes it brilliantly: not just one boy, but specifically a SMALL one. The specificity of 'small' is the funniest possible answer — it raises questions about why the boy's size matters, whether a large boy counts differently, and implies a very particular unit of labor measurement. Economy is exceptional.

jokes.text: So, for the Garden Weasel... this is Farmer Kingsley and... / Farmer Sanders. / Saying... / You all come back now, you hear?
jokes.setup: Hank wraps up the commercial with his 'Farmer Kingsley' sign-off
jokes.punchline: 'Farmer Sanders' — Larry reluctantly accepting the farmer persona — followed by 'You all come back now, you hear?' delivered in Southern accents, two Hollywood celebrities performing as yokels to sell a garden tool
jokes.explanation: The 'Farmer' personas are a nice absurdist touch — Hank and Larry as country gentlemen. The Beverly Hillbillies-style sign-off is an industry pastiche. Decent but not the sharpest joke in the sequence.

jokes.text: There you go, Shel. Television at its finest, huh? / It works, Larry. / Well, I'll tell ya, Hank's a master at these things. He is! / This is the way I think these commercials should be done. Exactly. This is why the Garden Weasel people want you to do more of you and Hank together. The two of you, as a team, you're fabulous.
jokes.setup: Sheldon praises the Hank/Larry commercial; Melanie endorses the team going forward
jokes.punchline: The commercial works — but only because Hank was brought in to rescue Larry's disaster. The irony that Larry started by trying to prevent Hank from doing commercials and ends up being the sidekick in Hank's success is the situational punch.
jokes.explanation: The structural irony of Larry being subordinated to Hank in the commercial pays off the episode's arc. Not a joke with a punchline so much as a thematic observation — the comedy is in recognizing the reversal.

jokes.text: Look, Shel, there's something I want to say about doing the commercials with Hank, and I want... / What Larry's gonna say is... / No, no, Artie. What I'm gonna say is no. I can't do these commercials. This has gone on long enough. I'm not comfortable doing these. By the way, unless we're all fucking blind, I stink at doing them.
jokes.setup: Larry is finally ready to put his foot down about the commercials; Artie tries to manage him
jokes.punchline: 'Unless we're all fucking blind, I stink at doing them' — Larry's final act of self-awareness delivered as his strongest argument, which is also a self-indictment
jokes.explanation: 'Unless we're all fucking blind, I stink at doing them' is a good Larry line — his self-awareness about his terrible commercial performance is framed as obvious proof that doesn't need arguing. The directness is both funny and character-authentic.

jokes.text: And if Unidac Electronics has a little problem with this, they can screw a lightbulb up my ass and use me as a desk lamp.
jokes.setup: Larry declares independence from the network/parent company demands
jokes.punchline: The specific image of being used as a desk lamp via lightbulb-up-ass is Larry's most vulgar and specific expression of defiance in the episode
jokes.explanation: The callback to Unidac Electronics pays off with the most colorful insult in the episode. 'Screw a lightbulb up my ass and use me as a desk lamp' is a highly specific and original image. The electronics company producing lightbulbs (products they presumably make) being used to power Larry as office furniture is an absurdly precise escalation. High quotability.

jokes.text: Any thoughts? / No, but I'd like to... / I'm not sure anyone wants to hear what you gotta say, young lady.
jokes.setup: After Larry's defiant speech, Artie opens the floor; Melanie tries to respond
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately shuts Melanie down with 'I'm not sure anyone wants to hear what you gotta say, young lady' — the 'young lady' framing making it both condescending and cartoonishly rude
jokes.explanation: Artie's protective rudeness toward Melanie is consistent with his character. 'Young lady' is a perfect choice — it's dismissive without being overtly threatening, unlike his earlier Korea threats. The paternalism of the phrasing lands well.

jokes.text: Don't take this as a threat, but I killed a man like you in Korea, hand to hand. / My boy doesn't want to do any more commercials. From now on, you'll talk to me.
jokes.setup: Artie delivers his final statement to Sheldon, the network president
jokes.punchline: Artie extends his Korea kill mythology to Sheldon — 'I killed a MAN like you in Korea' (not a woman, notably) — and then delivers the actual business point ('my boy doesn't want to do commercials') in the same breath, making the murder-threat and the talent management note equivalent
jokes.explanation: The perfect capstone to the Korea running gag. 'Don't take this as a threat' before a direct threat is a great construction. 'A man like you' specifies Sheldon's type as killable, which is somehow more threatening than 'I'll kill you.' Then the pivot to 'my boy doesn't want to do commercials' makes the murder threat and the talent negotiation continuous — Artie's management style includes the implicit possibility of violence. This is Rip Torn's character fully realized in one speech.

jokes.text: Don't take this as a threat, but I killed a man like you in Korea, hand to hand. My boy doesn't want to do any more commercials. From now on, you'll talk to me. Understood, my friend, Shel?
jokes.setup: Artie taking charge of the situation with Sheldon
jokes.punchline: 'Don't take this as a threat, but I killed a man like you in Korea, hand to hand' — the Korea-killing gag applied now directly to Sheldon, with the absurdist qualifier 'don't take this as a threat' before a literal threat
jokes.explanation: The culmination and best instance of the episode's defining running gag. 'Don't take this as a threat, but I killed a man like you in Korea, hand to hand' is a perfect paradox: the disclaimer makes the threat more rather than less threatening, and 'a man like you' applies the template to a new victim while 'hand to hand' adds specific tactical detail that should not be there. The running gag has escalated perfectly — from reported line (joke 31) to Artie defending its sincerity (joke 49) to direct deployment (here). 'Understood, my friend, Shel?' as a closing demand is a beautiful bit of menacing politeness. One of the episode's finest moments and the strongest instance of the series' defining comic device.

jokes.text: You sure? / Sure. Don't worry about anything. / Sheldon, if you really want to try this once or twice, no problem. / Really? / Artie?
jokes.setup: Sheldon reassures Larry there's no problem; Artie suddenly reverses course and offers to do the commercial once or twice
jokes.punchline: Larry's baffled 'Artie?' — after Artie just delivered the most forceful refusal of the episode, he immediately offers to accommodate the network, revealing that the whole stand was theater and the real terms are negotiated separately
jokes.explanation: A good closing joke that undermines everything Larry just said. The comedy is structural — the big defiant speech immediately followed by Artie quietly giving the network what they want reveals that Artie's loyalty to Larry includes managing Larry's illusions about his own power. Larry's 'Artie?' is the perfect final note — bewildered, deflated, and somehow still clueless. A satisfying ironic button for the episode.

tmdb_overview: Over Larry's strong protests, network executives force him to do a live commercial on the show for one of his sponsors.
